text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Higgins v. Willis et al.,

2003 BCSC 1850

Date: 20031209

Docket:
S30885

Registry: Vernon

Between:

William H. Higgins

Plaintiff

And

David P.
Willis, Willis Higgins Building Corporation,

Willis Higgins Inc. and Sycamore Ventures Ltd.

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Barrow

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

D.M.
Rush

Counsel for the
Defendant, David Willis:

W.C.
Shields

Date and Place of Trial/Hearing:

December
1, 2003

Kelowna,
B.C.

[
1
]

This is an application by the defendant, David Willis,
for an order that this action be stayed until the plaintiff, William Higgins,
posts security for costs.  Because the plaintiff is a person (as opposed to a
corporation) the motion is brought pursuant to the court’s inherent
jurisdiction.

Factual Context

[
2
]

From 1990 until December 31, 2000, Mr. Willis and Mr.
Higgins, both of whom are chartered accountants, practiced together as partners
in Vernon, delivering tax and accounting advice to their clients under the firm
name of Willis Higgins Chartered Accountants.  The firm operated from premises
in a commercial building owned by Willis Higgins Building Corporation.  The
voting shares in that company are owned equally by Mr. Willis and Mr. Higgins.  Willis
Higgins Building Corporation is a defendant in this action.  Mr. Willis, in
addition to being a chartered accountant, is also a licensed trustee in
bankruptcy.  He is the sole shareholder in Willis Higgins Inc., which is also a
defendant in this action.

[
3
]

Following the breakdown of the partnership, both
Mr. Willis and Mr. Higgins continued to carry on their practices out of
the same premises, although they did so as separate and independent entities.  A
variety of disputes arose between them.  It is alleged by Mr. Willis that Mr.
Higgins failed to pay rent to Willis Higgins Building Corporation for his use
of office space in the building.  Because both Mr. Willis and Mr. Higgins
controlled the company equally, Mr. Willis petitioned the court for leave to
commence an action on behalf of the company to recover the rent said to be due.
Leave was granted and, I am advised, an action was commenced on August 20,
2002, in the Kelowna Registry.

[
4
]

On the same day the within action was commenced out of
the Vernon Registry.  In this action, Mr. Higgins seeks various forms of
relief.  He alleges that he and Mr. Willis had agreed that upon dissolution,
the firm’s assets and liabilities would be evenly divided.  He alleges that Mr.
Willis has refused to do that.  Further, he alleges that a variety of expenses
that Mr. Willis incurred and attributed to the partnership were not, in fact,
partnership expenses.  He alleges that Mr. Willis has borrowed against the firm’s
credit after the parties had agreed to dissolve the partnership.  He alleges
that Mr. Willis has refused to divide or account for any work in progress at
the time of dissolution, and that he has refused to divide or account for any
accounts receivable outstanding at the time of dissolution.  There is also a
dispute about the alleged improper use of Yellow Pages advertising.  Mr.
Higgins alleges that Mr. Willis improperly gave preferential treatment to an
employee of the firm, including causing the firm to pay for her several
attempts to achieve her C.A. designation, while Mr. Willis was, unknown to Mr.
Higgins, carrying on a romantic liaison with her.  There is an allegation that,
since the dissolution, an employee of Mr. Willis’ has been soliciting clients
of Mr. Higgins in an effort to have them redirect their business.  In
addition, Mr. Higgins claims that Mr. Willis has defamed him.  Finally, he
advances a number of claims against the various corporate entities in which the
former partners have an interest, seeking in most cases an order that the various
companies be wound up.

[
5
]

Mr. Willis has filed a statement of defence and a counterclaim.
In his statement of defence, he alleges that Mr. Higgins conducted himself
unprofessionally and improperly in the office, thus disrupting the business of
the partnership.  He alleges that Mr. Higgins pursued interests outside the
partnership for his own benefit, that he received benefits and assets from the
partnership for which he has failed to account, and generally failed to devote
himself to the partnership business.  In addition, it is alleged that Mr.
Higgins harassed employees of the partnership while granting favourable
treatment to his girlfriend, who was also an employee of the firm.  As to the
claims against the corporations, the defendant, Mr. Willis, denies any improper
conduct and says that it is the plaintiff, Mr. Higgins, who has failed to
honour his obligations towards some of these companies.  Mr. Willis alleges
that the plaintiff breached the partnership agreement, breached his fiduciary
obligations and his statutory obligations, and seeks to have the remedies to
which these breaches entitle him setoff against any remedy to which the
plaintiff might be entitled.

[
6
]

By the counterclaim, Mr. Willis repeats the allegations
in his statement of defence and seeks damages, an accounting, and an order
disposing of the firm’s assets.

The Law

[
7
]

The court has the inherent jurisdiction to order
security for costs against an individual (
Tordoff
v.
Canada Life
Assurance Co.
,
1985 CanLII 492 (BC SC)
, [1985] B.C.J. No. 2800 (S.C.) at para.
14
).  It is a
jurisdiction that is to be used “with great caution” (
Gray
v.

Powerassist Technologies Inc.
,
2001 BCSC 1208 (CanLII)
, [2001] B.C.J. No. 1722 (S.C.) at para.

20
).  It is only to be invoked “sparingly” (
Tordoff
, at para.
14
).
The jurisdiction to award security for costs against a corporate party is found
in
s. 205
of the
Company Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 62.  The
discretion conferred on the court by that section is broader than the
discretion the court has to order security for costs in relation to
individuals.  The reason for this distinction flows from the rationale for the
rule as it relates to corporations.  As Joyce J. put it in
Gray

at para.
20
:

The rationale behind the statutory provision concerning
corporations is to provide protection to defendants from abuse by natural persons
funding litigation brought by impecunious corporations, while standing behind
the corporate veil and taking the benefit of impunity from any personal
liability for costs.  That rationale is not present in the case of the
individual plaintiff.  He is exposed to an order for costs.  In the English
case of
Pearson v. Naydler
,
[1977] 3 All E.R. 531 (Ch.Div.)
,
referred to in
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.
, supra,
Vice Chancellor Megarry said at p. 533:

The basic rule that a natural
person who sues will not be ordered to give security for costs, however poor he
is, is ancient and well-established.  As Bowen LJ said in
Cowell v.
Taylor
[
(1885), 31 Ch.D. 34 at 38
], both at law and in equity 'the
general rule is that poverty is no bar to a litigant'.  The power to require
security for costs ought not to be used so as to bar even the poorest man from
the courts.

[
8
]

In order for the provisions of
s. 205
of the
Company
Act
to be engaged, a defendant has the obligation of demonstrating, at
least on a
prima facie
basis, that the plaintiff would be unable to pay
the defendant’s costs in the event the plaintiff’s action were to fail.  If the
applicant has satisfied this first hurdle, the plaintiff may still avoid an
order for security for costs by showing that it has sufficient exigible assets
to satisfy any potential award of costs.  Further, the plaintiff may avoid such
an order if it can show that there is no arguable defence to its claim (
Fat
Mel’s Restaurant Ltd.
v.
Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.

(1993),
1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (2d) 231 (C.A.) at para.
16
and
Citizens for Foreign
Aid Reform Inc.
v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No.
2160 (S.C.).  The same threshold considerations should apply to the exercise of
the court’s inherent jurisdiction in relation to individual plaintiffs.

[
9
]

Once the threshold for consideration of an order for
security for costs has been established and the court’s discretion engaged, an
order should only be granted in very limited circumstances taking into account,
among other things, the various factors summarized in
Kropp v. Swaneset
Bay Golf Course Ltd.

(1997), 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 352 (C.A.) at para. 17
.

Application to the Facts

[
10
]

I am not satisfied that the applicant has shown on a
prima facie

basis that the plaintiff would be unable to pay the defendant’s costs if the
plaintiff is unsuccessful (those costs have been estimated at approximately
$47,000).  He is employed as a chartered accountant, and there is no reason to
expect that he will not continue to be employed in that capacity.  He maintains
that he recently purchased a home for $314,000 in which he has $100,000 in
equity.  The applicant notes that there is no documentation to support these
assertions.  While that is so, as matters stand now, the assertion is
questioned but not contradicted.  On its own, this is sufficient to warrant the
dismissal of this application.

[
11
]

The applicant argues that, in an earlier application in the related
action started by Willis Higgins Building Corporation, the plaintiff indicated
that he was experiencing financial and personal difficulties.  I have no
evidence before me about that.  Moreover, the application in which the remarks
are said to have been made took place more than six months ago and is of little
assistance in assessing the plaintiff’s present circumstances.

[
12
]

Of greater significance, however, is the need for the partnership
affairs to be resolved.  Attempts to resolve them by way of mediation have, so
far, been unsuccessful.  Both Mr. Willis and Mr. Higgins are seeking similar
relief in the action in question - Mr. Higgins as plaintiff and Mr. Willis as
plaintiff by counterclaim.  To require Mr. Higgins to post security or face a
stay of his claim, while Mr. Willis remains at liberty to pursue essentially
the very same relief, would work an injustice.  For that reason alone, I would
not exercise the discretion I have to make the order sought by Mr. Willis.

[
13
]

In all of the circumstances, the application for security for costs
is dismissed.  Costs will be left to the discretion of the trial judge.

”G.M. Barrow, J.”

The
Honourable Mr. Justice G.M. Barrow
